title: When the Orange's Face Flies Off
author: Andrew Ellison
source: Classical Ed Review on Substack, December 19, 2025
summary: Ellison argues that early Sesame Street vignettes succeeded by respecting children's capacity for genuine intellectual engagement. Three-to-five minute segments on how saxophones are made or how bread is baked held attention because they were inherently interesting, not because of animation or catchy songs. Modern 'developmentally appropriate' theory claims children cannot sustain attention and need constant rapid input, but this view lacks evidence and justifies dumbing down content. Children can attend to what is genuinely worth attending to, and education that respects this capacity produces better results than education treating the child's mind as a perpetual video game.
points: Children are capable of real attention: The classical view that kids will focus on genuinely interesting material holds up better than theories about developmental limitations.
Theory-driven dumbing down: Modern 'developmentally appropriate' instruction lacks evidence but has justified progressively shorter, faster, more colorful content.
Inherent interest drives learning: Sesame Street's best work made things fascinating without animation or music, trusting the subject matter itself.
Long-term outcomes favor substance: Education respecting children's growing intellectual capacity produces better results than constant stimulation.
quotes: Sesame Street's original vignettes were charming creative insights: how a saxophone works, how bread is baked, how oranges are harvested. Each was brief but not trivial, interesting because it was genuinely interesting, not because it was set to a catchy tune or wrapped in a cartoon.

The prevailing theory of 'developmentally appropriate' instruction holds that a child's mind is incapable of sustained attention. Educationists have called this consciousness a 'Heraclitan flux of images and impressions,' a perpetual stream of fleeting perceptions.

The classical view trusts that children are capable of real intellectual engagement if the material genuinely merits attention. A baker falling down the stairs with cakes does not need animation, rapid cutting, or music to be interesting; it is inherently interesting.
Educational content that respects children's growing capacity for sustained thought and genuine understanding produces better long-term results than content designed for fragmented attention.
The question is not whether children can attend, but what is worth attending to.” Archived from Classical Ed Review on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
